title: These AI Barons Are Ready to Give Away Their Fortunes
excerpt: A new generation of philanthropists made rich by artificial intelligence are preparing to give away their vast wealth. What should we make of a multi-billion-dollar pinky promise?
content_html:
David Silver is a billionaire, sort of. His stake in Ineffable Intelligence—the artificial intelligence lab he founded—is worth an ungodly fortune. But he stands to collect none of that money himself. He set things up that way.

Between 2013 and 2025, Silver worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He specialized in reinforcement learning, a method of teaching an AI model through positive and negative feedback. In 2016, he led the development of AlphaGo, which became the first AI to defeat a human champion in the game of Go and was heralded as a narrow form of superintelligence. Silver left to start Ineffable Intelligence in January, betting that reinforcement learning breakthroughs will close the gap between human and machine cognition across the board.

When he started Ineffable Intelligence, Silver raised $1.1 billion from investors at a $5.1 billion valuation, reportedly the largest seed round in Europe’s history. He also vowed to donate all the money he makes from any future sale of his company to charity.

“I was thinking very deeply about what I could do to have the maximum impact on the world,” Silver tells WIRED in an interview at his office in Kings Cross, London, around the corner from DeepMind’s headquarters. “Not just through the work I do, but through the finance I arrive at in the process.”

He’ll choose how to deploy the funds after he sells his company, he says, but his ambition is to save as many lives as possible.

Silver is the latest in a growing line of AI founders to pledge equity proceeds to charity. Others include Mustafa Suleyman, a DeepMind cofounder and the CEO of AI at Microsoft, and Anton Osika, the founder of automated coding platform Lovable. If OpenAI and Anthropic go public as planned, minting thousands of new millionaires in the process, the AI industry could soon come to represent an increasingly outsize proportion of tech philanthropy.

Along with a new generation of techno-philanthropists, though, comes a tangle of unresolved questions: Is philanthropy the most appropriate way to redistribute wealth? To what degree are megadonors responsible for some of the problems they aim to fix? Could a pledge that scales with a company’s success come to justify unsavory business practices or reckless accelerationism? And is this go-around any different from previous iterations of Silicon Valley giving?

“You can’t necessarily appeal to capitalism to solve some of the problems created by capitalist practices themselves … the exacerbation of extreme wealth concentration and massive inequalities,” says Linsey McGoey, professor of sociology at the University of Essex and author of No Such Thing as a Free Gift. “It’s like calling upon the arsonist to hose down the house he’s just set on fire.”

Silver formalized his charitable commitment through Founders Pledge, a nonprofit that helps entrepreneurs to give away their wealth. Unlike the Giving Pledge, a public but nonbinding commitment, Founders Pledge requires participants to enter into a contract. “The choice of making a binding pledge was very important,” says Silver.

Founders Pledge has been around since 2015. But the value of pledges recorded by the nonprofit has soared recently, from $400 million in 2023 to $4 billion so far this year. The AI industry now accounts for a third of the lifetime pledge total.

The organization’s goal, according to cofounder David Goldberg, is to identify “the very best ways to deploy capital at scale to make the world better.” It has frequently been lumped together with effective altruism, which encourages people to amass wealth in order to give it away, to rely on statistics rather than emotion, and to prioritize causes likely to have the biggest impact in the distant future. But despite the commonalities, Goldberg isn’t a fan of the comparison; Founders Pledge is concerned with human suffering in the present. “We’re far more humanist,” he says.

Silver considers himself an effective altruist but says his “flavor is about the here and now.” Accordingly, Silver plans to funnel his pledge proceeds to charities, like the Malaria Foundation, equipped to save the greatest number of lives in the near term. “I find it hard to justify focusing on the galactic future of humanity when there are millions of people suffering and dying today,” he says.

Osika, the Lovable founder, who has pledged to give away half of his equity proceeds, doesn’t identify as an effective altruist, but he shares the belief that amassing wealth by succeeding in business is the best way for him to maximize his personal impact on the world. “I think it’s a very good thing for people who are very thoughtful about the future of humanity to build [AI],” he tells WIRED.

The Gates Foundation—the most famous embodiment of techno-philanthropy—has given away more than $100 billion to causes targeting poverty and disease in the 25 years since it was founded by Bill and Melinda Gates. Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have pledged to donate their $200 billion fortune to scientific research through their own foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. Both have been held up as shining examples of how an entrepreneurial mindset can translate into effective philanthropy and how the profit motive can be harnessed for good.

The new generation of AI philanthropists appear to want to carry that legacy forward, into a world they imagine will be utterly reorganized by superintelligence. “For a very long time, it’s been clear to me that this technological transformation is going to be the biggest thing that happens in our lives,” says Osika.

However, this type of giving can come with trade-offs, and can be used by megadonors to discreetly advance their political interests, McGoey says. A recent study found that a reliance on philanthropic funding led the WHO to prioritize donors’ preferred causes at the expense of other urgent issues, like non-communicable diseases.

Donations that alleviate issues stemming from wealth inequality instead of attacking the root cause, McGoey argues, threaten to end the debate about long-term, systemic remedies before it begins. “It’s appealing to the perpetuator of a problem to resolve it—and that doesn’t necessarily lead to positive results,” she says. “I don’t think that people should kid themselves that making money on its own is somehow noble.”

The WHO itself has acknowledged issues with its financing, and in 2022 it put forth a new model designed to address some of those concerns. Mark Suzman, the Gates Foundation’s CEO, has also recognized the pitfalls of relying on megadonors. “It’s not right for a private philanthropy to be one of the largest funders of multinational global health efforts,” he said in 2023, noting that the foundation had become the WHO’s second-largest donor. But he also put the blame on dwindling governmental contributions. “I’d love it if many more governments would pass us on that list,” he said.

Megadonors can play a valuable role in funding causes neglected for ideological reasons by governments, like family planning. But they’re not equally accountable, says Apolline Taillandier, a researcher at the University of Cambridge who specializes in political theory. “These funders are not elected. They have no need to account for their decisions,” she says. “It comes down to the question of whether philanthropy is the most legitimate way of redistributing resources.”

There is a further risk that entrepreneurs might treat their philanthropic ambition as moral justification for destructive behavior. In 2024, the one-time crypto kingpin and effective altruism poster boy Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud. At trial, a former colleague testified that Bankman-Fried had based all of his decisions on cold statistical analysis, gladly risking disaster if it meant a chance at a sufficiently positive end result. The leaders of effective altruism declared Bankman-Friend an apostate, but others painted his fraud as a symptom of the movement's flawed moral logic.

In the context of artificial intelligence, the concern is that a charitable pledge could form part of a risk calculation. By Bankman-Friedian logic, the headlong pursuit of superintelligence would be justified, potential consequences be damned, if the money it creates will have a large enough philanthropic impact.

Silver denies that his pledge is part of some sort of moral accounting or a hedge against the possible negative outcomes of the AI race. He believes that superintelligence will have a radically positive impact, endlessly discovering new knowledge through a recursive cycle of trial and error.

Far from justifying reckless accelerationism, Silver argues, a pledge helps to eliminate the type of financial incentive that threatens to lead AI development astray. “Building a superintelligence company is a huge responsibility to the planet, and that responsibility shouldn’t be led by personal greed,” says Silver. “This was an intentional choice to make sure that whatever actions I take as an individual are for the benefit of humanity, not because there’s some enormous dollar figure that starts to appear on the horizon.”

Silver may be a beneficiary of an economic system stacked in his favor. But one of few ways he can redress that imbalance, he argues, is to give his money away. “Individuals that choose to use their money for good will have a massive, transformative difference on the future of the world we live in,” he says. “That’s independent of whether the macroeconomic situation is the right thing for humanity. It’s just a fact.”

sentences.zh: 西尔弗认为自己是一个有效的利他主义者，但他说他的“品味就是此时此地”。

sentences.en: Accordingly, Silver plans to funnel his pledge proceeds to charities, like the Malaria Foundation, equipped to save the greatest number of lives in the near term.
sentences.zh: 因此，西尔弗计划将他的认捐所得捐献给疟疾基金会等慈善机构，以便在短期内挽救最多的生命。

sentences.en: “I find it hard to justify focusing on the galactic future of humanity when there are millions of people suffering and dying today,” he says.
sentences.zh: “当今天有数百万人正在受苦和死亡时，我发现很难证明关注人类银河系的未来是合理的，”他说。

blocks.html_en: Osika, the Lovable founder, who has pledged to give away half of his equity proceeds, doesn’t identify as an effective altruist, but he shares the belief that amassing wealth by succeeding in business is the best way for him to maximize his personal impact on the world. “I think it’s a very good thing for people who are very thoughtful about the future of humanity to build [AI],” he tells WIRED.

sentences.en: Osika, the Lovable founder, who has pledged to give away half of his equity proceeds, doesn’t identify as an effective altruist, but he shares the belief that amassing wealth by succeeding in business is the best way for him to maximize his personal impact on the world.
sentences.zh: Lovable 创始人 Osika 承诺捐出一半的股权收益，他并不认为自己是一个有效的利他主义者，但他也相信，通过商业成功积累财富是他最大限度地发挥个人对世界影响力的最佳方式。

sentences.en: “I think it’s a very good thing for people who are very thoughtful about the future of humanity to build [AI],” he tells WIRED.

blocks.html_en: The Gates Foundation—the most famous embodiment of techno-philanthropy—has given away more than $100 billion to causes targeting poverty and disease in the 25 years since it was founded by Bill and Melinda Gates. Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have pledged to donate their $200 billion fortune to scientific research through their own foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. Both have been held up as shining examples of how an entrepreneurial mindset can translate into effective philanthropy and how the profit motive can be harnessed for good.

sentences.en: The Gates Foundation—the most famous embodiment of techno-philanthropy—has given away more than $100 billion to causes targeting poverty and disease in the 25 years since it was founded by Bill and Melinda Gates.
sentences.zh: 盖茨基金会——科技慈善事业最著名的体现——自比尔·盖茨和梅琳达·盖茨创立 25 年来，已向贫困和疾病事业捐赠了超过 1000 亿美元。

sentences.en: Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have pledged to donate their $200 billion fortune to scientific research through their own foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.

blocks.html_en: The new generation of AI philanthropists appear to want to carry that legacy forward, into a world they imagine will be utterly reorganized by superintelligence. “For a very long time, it’s been clear to me that this technological transformation is going to be the biggest thing that happens in our lives,” says Osika.

sentences.en: The new generation of AI philanthropists appear to want to carry that legacy forward, into a world they imagine will be utterly reorganized by superintelligence.

sentences.zh: 最近的一项研究发现，对慈善资金的依赖导致世界卫生组织优先考虑捐助者首选的事业，而牺牲了非传染性疾病等其他紧急问题。

blocks.html_en: Donations that alleviate issues stemming from wealth inequality instead of attacking the root cause, McGoey argues, threaten to end the debate about long-term, systemic remedies before it begins. “It’s appealing to the perpetuator of a problem to resolve it—and that doesn’t necessarily lead to positive results,” she says. “I don’t think that people should kid themselves that making money on its own is somehow noble.”

sentences.en: Donations that alleviate issues stemming from wealth inequality instead of attacking the root cause, McGoey argues, threaten to end the debate about long-term, systemic remedies before it begins.
sentences.zh: 麦戈伊认为，旨在缓解财富不平等问题而不是解决根本原因的捐款可能会在有关长期、系统性补救措施的辩论开始之前就结束了。

sentences.zh: “这对问题的持续存在者来说很有吸引力，希望能够解决它，但这并不一定会带来积极的结果，”她说。

sentences.en: “I don’t think that people should kid themselves that making money on its own is somehow noble.”
sentences.zh: “我认为人们不应该欺骗自己，认为自己赚钱在某种程度上是高尚的。”

blocks.html_en: The WHO itself has acknowledged issues with its financing, and in 2022 it put forth a new model designed to address some of those concerns. Mark Suzman, the Gates Foundation’s CEO, has also recognized the pitfalls of relying on megadonors. “It’s not right for a private philanthropy to be one of the largest funders of multinational global health efforts,” he said in 2023, noting that the foundation had become the WHO’s second-largest donor. But he also put the blame on dwindling governmental contributions. “I’d love it if many more governments would pass us on that list,” he said.

sentences.en: The WHO itself has acknowledged issues with its financing, and in 2022 it put forth a new model designed to address some of those concerns.
sentences.zh: 世界卫生组织本身也承认其融资存在问题，并于 2022 年提出了一种新模式，旨在解决其中一些问题。

sentences.en: Mark Suzman, the Gates Foundation’s CEO, has also recognized the pitfalls of relying on megadonors.
sentences.zh: 盖茨基金会首席执行官马克·苏兹曼也认识到依赖巨额捐助者的陷阱。

sentences.en: “It’s not right for a private philanthropy to be one of the largest funders of multinational global health efforts,” he said in 2023, noting that the foundation had become the WHO’s second-largest donor.
sentences.zh: 他在 2023 年表示：“私人慈善机构成为跨国全球卫生努力的最大资助者之一是不正确的。”他指出，该基金会已成为世界卫生组织的第二大捐助者。

sentences.en: But he also put the blame on dwindling governmental contributions.
sentences.zh: 但他也将责任归咎于政府捐款的减少。

sentences.en: “I’d love it if many more governments would pass us on that list,” he said.
sentences.zh: 他说：“如果有更多的政府将我们列入这份名单，我会很高兴。”

blocks.html_en: Megadonors can play a valuable role in funding causes neglected for ideological reasons by governments, like family planning. But they’re not equally accountable, says Apolline Taillandier, a researcher at the University of Cambridge who specializes in political theory. “These funders are not elected. They have no need to account for their decisions,” she says. “It comes down to the question of whether philanthropy is the most legitimate way of redistributing resources.”

sentences.zh: 巨额捐助者可以在资助因意识形态原因而被政府忽视的事业（例如计划生育）方面发挥重要作用。

sentences.en: But they’re not equally accountable, says Apolline Taillandier, a researcher at the University of Cambridge who specializes in political theory.
sentences.zh: 但剑桥大学专门研究政治理论的研究员阿波琳·泰兰迪尔表示，他们的责任并不相同。

sentences.en: “These funders are not elected.
sentences.zh: “这些资助者不是选举产生的。

sentences.en: They have no need to account for their decisions,” she says.
sentences.zh: 他们不需要为自己的决定负责，”她说。

sentences.en: “It comes down to the question of whether philanthropy is the most legitimate way of redistributing resources.”
sentences.zh: “这归根结底是慈善事业是否是重新分配资源的最合法方式的问题。”

blocks.html_en: There is a further risk that entrepreneurs might treat their philanthropic ambition as moral justification for destructive behavior. In 2024, the one-time crypto kingpin and effective altruism poster boy Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud. At trial, a former colleague testified that Bankman-Fried had based all of his decisions on cold statistical analysis, gladly risking disaster if it meant a chance at a sufficiently positive end result. The leaders of effective altruism declared Bankman-Friend an apostate, but others painted his fraud as a symptom of the movement's flawed moral logic.

blocks.html_en: Silver denies that his pledge is part of some sort of moral accounting or a hedge against the possible negative outcomes of the AI race. He believes that superintelligence will have a radically positive impact, endlessly discovering new knowledge through a recursive cycle of trial and error.

sentences.en: Silver denies that his pledge is part of some sort of moral accounting or a hedge against the possible negative outcomes of the AI race.
sentences.zh: 西尔弗否认他的承诺是某种道德核算的一部分，或者是对人工智能竞赛可能产生的负面结果的对冲。

sentences.en: He believes that superintelligence will have a radically positive impact, endlessly discovering new knowledge through a recursive cycle of trial and error.
sentences.zh: 他认为超级智能将产生根本性的积极影响，通过反复试验和错误的递归循环不断发现新知识。

blocks.html_en: Far from justifying reckless accelerationism, Silver argues, a pledge helps to eliminate the type of financial incentive that threatens to lead AI development astray. “Building a superintelligence company is a huge responsibility to the planet, and that responsibility shouldn’t be led by personal greed,” says Silver. “This was an intentional choice to make sure that whatever actions I take as an individual are for the benefit of humanity, not because there’s some enormous dollar figure that starts to appear on the horizon.”

sentences.zh: 西尔弗认为，这一承诺远非为鲁莽的加速主义辩护，而是有助于消除可能导致人工智能发展误入歧途的经济激励措施。

sentences.en: “Building a superintelligence company is a huge responsibility to the planet, and that responsibility shouldn’t be led by personal greed,” says Silver.
sentences.zh: “建立一家超级智能公司是对地球的巨大责任，而这种责任不应该由个人贪婪来主导，”西尔弗说。

sentences.en: “This was an intentional choice to make sure that whatever actions I take as an individual are for the benefit of humanity, not because there’s some enormous dollar figure that starts to appear on the horizon.”
sentences.zh: “这是一个有意的选择，以确保我作为个人采取的任何行动都是为了人类的利益，而不是因为即将出现一些巨大的美元数字。”

sentences.zh: 这只是一个事实。”

content_html_zh:
大卫·西尔弗（David Silver）可以说是一位亿万富翁。 他在 Ineffable Intelligence（他创立的人工智能实验室）中的股份价值不菲。 但他本人不会收取任何费用。 他就是这样安排的。

2013 年至 2025 年间，Silver 在 Google DeepMind 担任研究员。 他专门研究强化学习，这是一种通过正反馈和负反馈来教授人工智能模型的方法。 2016年，他领导开发了AlphaGo，成为第一个在围棋比赛中击败人类冠军的人工智能，并被誉为狭义的超级智能。 西尔弗于一月份离职，创立了 Ineffable Intelligence，他坚信强化学习的突破将全面缩小人类和机器认知之间的差距。

当西尔弗创办 Ineffable Intelligence 时，他以 51 亿美元的估值从投资者那里筹集了 11 亿美元，据报道这是欧洲历史上最大的种子轮融资。 他还发誓要将未来出售公司所得的所有资金捐献给慈善机构。

“我非常深入地思考我可以做些什么来对世界产生最大的影响，”西尔弗在他位于伦敦国王十字的办公室接受采访时告诉《连线》，该办公室距离 DeepMind 总部不远。 “不仅通过我所做的工作，还通过我在此过程中获得的财务。”

他说，他将在出售公司后选择如何部署这些资金，但他的目标是拯救尽可能多的生命。

越来越多的人工智能创始人将股权收益承诺捐赠给慈善机构，西尔弗是其中最新的一位。 其他人包括 DeepMind 联合创始人兼微软人工智能首席执行官 Mustafa Suleyman 和自动编码平台 Lovable 创始人 Anton Osika。 如果 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 按计划上市，并在此过程中创造数千名新的百万富翁，那么人工智能行业可能很快就会在科技慈善事业中占据越来越大的比例。

然而，伴随新一代技术慈善家而来的是一系列悬而未决的问题：慈善事业是财富重新分配的最合适方式吗？ 巨额捐助者在多大程度上对他们旨在解决的一些问题负有责任？ 随着公司的成功而做出的承诺是否可以证明令人厌恶的商业行为或鲁莽的加速主义是合理的？ 这次的转变与硅谷之前的捐赠有什么不同吗？

“你不一定能诉诸资本主义来解决资本主义实践本身造成的一些问题…… 埃塞克斯大学社会学教授、《没有免费的礼物》一书的作者林赛·麦戈伊 (Linsey McGoey) 表示：“财富极端集中和严重不平等的加剧。” “这就像要求纵火犯用水管冲洗他刚刚放火的房子。”

西尔弗通过创始人承诺（Founders Pledge）正式履行了他的慈善承诺，这是一个帮助企业家捐赠财富的非营利组织。 与捐赠誓言这种公开但不具约束力的承诺不同，创始人誓言要求参与者签订合同。 “做出具有约束力的承诺的选择非常重要，”西尔弗说。

创始人承诺自 2015 年以来一直存在。 但该非营利组织记录的承诺价值最近飙升，从 2023 年的 4 亿美元增至今年迄今的 40 亿美元。 人工智能行业目前占终身承诺总额的三分之一。

联合创始人大卫·戈德堡表示，该组织的目标是找到“大规模部署资本以使世界变得更美好的最佳方式”。 它经常与有效的利他主义混为一谈，后者鼓励人们积累财富以便捐赠，依赖统计数据而不是情感，并优先考虑可能在遥远的未来产生最大影响的事业。 尽管有共同点，戈德堡并不喜欢这种比较。创始人誓言关注当前人类的苦难。 “我们更加人文主义，”他说。

西尔弗认为自己是一个有效的利他主义者，但他说他的“品味就是此时此地”。 因此，西尔弗计划将他的认捐所得捐献给疟疾基金会等慈善机构，以便在短期内挽救最多的生命。 “当今天有数百万人正在受苦和死亡时，我发现很难证明关注人类银河系的未来是合理的，”他说。

Lovable 创始人 Osika 承诺捐出一半的股权收益，他并不认为自己是一个有效的利他主义者，但他也相信，通过商业成功积累财富是他最大限度地发挥个人对世界影响力的最佳方式。 他告诉《连线》杂志：“我认为，对于那些对人类未来深思熟虑的人来说，构建人工智能是一件非常好的事情。”

盖茨基金会——科技慈善事业最著名的体现——自比尔·盖茨和梅琳达·盖茨创立 25 年来，已向贫困和疾病事业捐赠了超过 1000 亿美元。 Meta 创始人马克·扎克伯格 (Mark Zuckerberg) 和他的妻子普里西拉·陈 (Priscilla Chan) 承诺通过他们自己的基金会“陈·扎克伯格倡议”(Chan Zuckerberg Initiative) 捐赠 2000 亿美元的财富用于科学研究。 两者都被视为创业思维如何转化为有效的慈善事业以及如何利用利润动机进行善行的光辉典范。

新一代人工智能慈善家似乎希望将这一遗产发扬光大，进入一个他们想象的将被超级智能彻底重组的世界。 “很长一段时间以来，我一直很清楚，这种技术变革将成为我们生活中发生的最重大的事情，”奥西卡说。

然而，这种类型的捐赠可能需要权衡，并且可以被超级捐赠者用来谨慎地推进他们的政治利益，麦戈伊说。 最近的一项研究发现，对慈善资金的依赖导致世界卫生组织优先考虑捐助者首选的事业，而牺牲了非传染性疾病等其他紧急问题。

麦戈伊认为，旨在缓解财富不平等问题而不是解决根本原因的捐款可能会在有关长期、系统性补救措施的辩论开始之前就结束了。 “这对问题的持续存在者来说很有吸引力，希望能够解决它，但这并不一定会带来积极的结果，”她说。 “我认为人们不应该欺骗自己，认为自己赚钱在某种程度上是高尚的。”

世界卫生组织本身也承认其融资存在问题，并于 2022 年提出了一种新模式，旨在解决其中一些问题。 盖茨基金会首席执行官马克·苏兹曼也认识到依赖巨额捐助者的陷阱。 他在 2023 年表示：“私人慈善机构成为跨国全球卫生努力的最大资助者之一是不正确的。”他指出，该基金会已成为世界卫生组织的第二大捐助者。 但他也将责任归咎于政府捐款的减少。 他说：“如果有更多的政府将我们列入这份名单，我会很高兴。”

巨额捐助者可以在资助因意识形态原因而被政府忽视的事业（例如计划生育）方面发挥重要作用。 但剑桥大学专门研究政治理论的研究员阿波琳·泰兰迪尔表示，他们的责任并不相同。 “这些资助者不是选举产生的。 他们不需要为自己的决定负责，”她说。 “这归根结底是慈善事业是否是重新分配资源的最合法方式的问题。”

还有一个进一步的风险，即企业家可能将他们的慈善野心视为破坏性行为的道德理由。 2024 年，曾经的加密货币大佬、利他主义的典型代表 Sam Bankman-Fried 因欺诈被判处 25 年监禁。 在审判中，一位前同事作证说，班克曼-弗里德的所有决定都是基于冷酷的统计分析，如果这意味着有机会获得足够积极的最终结果，他很乐意冒着灾难的风险。 有效利他主义的领导人宣称班克曼·弗兰德是叛教者，但其他人则将他的欺诈行为描述为该运动道德逻辑有缺陷的症状。

在人工智能的背景下，人们担心慈善承诺可能成为风险计算的一部分。 按照班克曼-弗里迪安的逻辑，如果超级智能创造的资金能够产生足够大的慈善影响，那么对超级智能的盲目追求是合理的，但潜在的后果却是可悲的。

西尔弗否认他的承诺是某种道德核算的一部分，或者是对人工智能竞赛可能产生的负面结果的对冲。 他认为超级智能将产生根本性的积极影响，通过反复试验和错误的递归循环不断发现新知识。

西尔弗认为，这一承诺远非为鲁莽的加速主义辩护，而是有助于消除可能导致人工智能发展误入歧途的经济激励措施。 “建立一家超级智能公司是对地球的巨大责任，而这种责任不应该由个人贪婪来主导，”西尔弗说。 “这是一个有意的选择，以确保我作为个人采取的任何行动都是为了人类的利益，而不是因为即将出现一些巨大的美元数字。”

白银可能是对他有利的经济体系的受益者。 但他认为，纠正这种不平衡的方法之一就是捐出自己的钱。 “选择将钱用于行善的个人将对我们生活的世界的未来产生巨大的、变革性的影响，”他说。 “这与宏观经济形势是否对人类有利无关。 这只是一个事实。”
